name: LangChain / LangGraph
summary: One stack from one vendor, rated together: LangChain for standardized model interfaces and the largest third-party integration catalog, LangGraph for durable stateful agent graphs, the LangGraph Platform Agent Server for assistants, threads, runs, and cron, and the commercial LangSmith for tracing and evals. The libraries are MIT and run wherever you host them; tracing, evals, and the hosted server are paid products.
license: MIT (LangChain, LangGraph); LangSmith and LangGraph Platform are commercial

agent-runtime.note: LangChain's agent abstractions on top of LangGraph's graph runtime, which executes stateful agent loops with durable execution and resumes from a checkpoint after a failure.

orchestration.note: Graphs mix deterministic and model-driven steps for multi-step and multi-agent workflows, and the Agent Server exposes assistants, threads, runs, and cron jobs over HTTP.

knowledge-memory.note: Vector store, retriever, and embedding abstractions over a large integration catalog, plus a cross-thread Store with optional semantic search. The storage engines are third-party, and neither library ships a document ingestion or chunking pipeline of its own.

tools-integration.note: Tool-calling abstractions and hundreds of third-party integrations; MCP servers connect through the separate langchain-mcp-adapters package.

identity-governance.note: Real approval gates via interrupts, and the Platform accepts custom auth handlers with resource filters — but the handlers are yours to write, and there is no quota enforcement, policy language, or audit log.

observability.note: Deep tracing and monitoring through LangSmith, a separate commercial product enabled by an environment variable rather than part of either library.

data-secrets.note: No managed file storage and no encrypted secrets store; persistence stops at checkpointers and the key-value Store, and credentials are the host application's problem.

evaluation.note: Datasets, evaluators, and experiment tracking live in the commercial LangSmith product, with the open-source openevals utilities alongside it; nothing gates a deployment on a result.

channels.note: No first-party messaging gateway and no bundled chat UI — the Agent Server speaks HTTP, and Slack or Discord delivery comes from community integrations or the host application.

code-execution.note: Sandboxed execution arrives as integration tools (E2B, Riza, Bearly) rather than a runtime either library operates.

human-in-loop.note: interrupt() checkpoints graph state and pauses a node indefinitely; Command(resume=value) re-invokes the same thread. HumanInTheLoopMiddleware wraps that in an interrupt_on map of tool names with approve, edit, and reject decisions.

multi-tenancy.note: Agent Server auth handlers can stamp owner metadata onto threads, runs, and assistants and filter reads by it, but there is no tenant or workspace object — the isolation is whatever those handlers implement.

declarative-deployment.note: langgraph.json declares the graphs, dependencies, and environment of a single deployed application. There is no plan and apply step and no dependency graph across resources.

agent-versioning.note: Each assistant update creates a new version that can be promoted to active or rolled back; there is no canary rollout and no eval-gated promotion.

skill-learning.note: The separate Deep Agents package exposes a skills parameter for procedural memory whose skill files an agent can write and edit itself. Core LangChain and LangGraph have no equivalent — the Store persists data, not reusable skills.
